title: Kerfless porous-silicon lift-off reuses each crystal-grown wafer tenfold
idea: Combine solar-industry epitaxial lift-off (porous-Si release layer under 20 um epitaxy) with DRAM. The memory is built in the epi layer, bonded device-side to a carrier or logic wafer, cleaved at the porous layer, and the CZ parent wafer is re-polished and reused 10+ times.
why: Cuts prime-wafer demand ~10x and with it the Spruce Pine (>80%) high-purity quartz crucible dependence. Wafer cost (~5-8% of DRAM cost) falls, and HBM thinning comes free (scarce resources, fact 6).

title: Liberty-ship DRAM: frozen open design built by many fabs
idea: Borrowed from WWII Liberty ships, one frozen simplified design built in 18 yards by non-specialists: a 10-person federal program office freezes a royalty-free 8 Gb DDR4-class 1T1C design on ~25 nm DUV with documented recipes and test programs, and licenses it with qualification support to any U.S. fab or foundry.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: removes the ~$500M+ design and IP barrier that keeps foundries out of commodity DRAM and creates surge capacity for critical supply.

title: Cross-laminated timber: rotate tier orientation to cancel wafer bow
idea: Borrowed from cross-laminated timber, which rotates the grain 90 degrees per layer so warping cancels: in stacked 3D DRAM, rotate wordline/bitline direction 90 degrees every N tiers and alternate tensile and compressive film stacks so anisotropic stress cancels, keeping bow under ~50 um at 64+ tiers.
why: Fact 2: wafer bow and overlay drift cap tier count and force backside stress films and extra correction steps; stress cancellation buys more tiers per litho set.

title: Core memory reborn as plated toroids around through-glass vias
idea: Revive 1950s coincident-current ferrite core memory on 515x510 mm glass panels: laser-modified, wet-etched through-glass vias at ~3 um pitch get an electroplated square-loop NiFeMo toroid, and the X, Y and sense wires become ordinary panel redistribution layers instead of hand-threaded wire. The panel is a passive array; drivers and sense amps sit on a small CMOS chiplet at its edge.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: panel-level packaging lines cost ~1/20 of a DRAM fab per m2 and need no EUV or sub-um litho. At ~10 Mb/cm2 per layer it is far below DRAM density, so the gain is refresh-free, non-volatile, radiation-hard bits from idle substrate capacity, not leading-edge cost per bit.

title: Glass-core HBM base replaces silicon interposer and TSV die
idea: Worse: spend 3x wafer area per bit and TSV yield losses on silicon interposers. Flip: build HBM base routing and through-vias in glass-core panels (laser-modified, wet-etched TGVs at ~10 um pitch) on 510x515 mm panel lines, and hybrid-bond the DRAM dies to the glass.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): frees the silicon interposer/base area at ~3-5x lower panel cost per area, with U.S. glass suppliers.

title: Desert-fab supercritical CO2 cleans replace ultrapure-water wet benches
idea: Extreme user: an Arizona fab with almost no water. Replace RCA/SPM wet cleans with supercritical CO2 plus alcohol/amine co-solvents and cryogenic CO2-aerosol particle removal, with residues stripped dry and CO2 recaptured.
why: Water/capital: cuts ultrapure-water demand ~50% and the UPW plant capex; no fluorinated surfactants or HF; no wet-drying pattern collapse.

title: Backside capacitors: storage nodes etched into the thinned wafer back
idea: Box: deep-trench charge x vertical-channel access x standard sensing x front/back split x thinned Si on carrier x backside trench etch self-aligned to buried drains. After front-side transistors and bitlines, the wafer is bonded face-down and thinned, and capacitor trenches are etched from the back into bulk Si landing on each transistor's buried drain, so capacitors no longer compete with bitlines for front-side space.
why: Removes storage-node-contact and landing-pad layers (2-3 masks incl. ~1 EUV) and gives free capacitor height (Cs >8 fF); reuses backside-power tools now entering logic fabs.

title: Pure-play foundry model with an open DRAM cell PDK
idea: Borrow TSMC's split of design from manufacturing: a DRAM foundry runs one qualified cell process with an open process design kit (cell, sense amp and redundancy libraries), and many fabless memory designers tape out custom DRAMs (AI-tuned page sizes, CXL, in-memory compute) on shared capacity.
why: Capital utilization and innovation: pooled demand keeps the fab full across cycles, and new memory products need design budgets (~$20-50M) instead of a $15B fab.

title: Area-selective deposition pattern propagation: zero-overlay layer stacking
idea: First principle: overlay error exists only because each layer is aligned optically; if each new layer nucleates only on a material exposed by the layer below (inhibitor SAMs that bind oxide but not metal, and the reverse), the pattern propagates chemically with zero misalignment. Design the cell so landing pads, contacts and the capacitor bottom electrode are each grown selectively on the previous layer, leaving one litho master for the array.
why: Litho and masks (fact 4): removes 2-3 critical masks and the overlay budget that limits 12 nm cells; tighter pitch without new optics.

title: Liquid-nitrogen DRAM: minutes of retention shrink the capacitor tenfold
idea: Time-shift retention via temperature: at 77 K leakage drops by orders of magnitude, so retention grows from ms to minutes; design the cell around a ~0.5 fF capacitor, delete the high-AR capacitor module, and deploy in U.S. datacenters cooled with domestic LN2 (no helium).
why: Removes the most expensive capacitor steps (Facts 1, 4) and nearly all refresh energy (Fact 3); cooling overhead is absorbed at rack scale.

title: Silicon-on-sapphire cells eliminate substrate junction leakage tail
idea: Worse: keep the storage-node junction in a bulk crystal whose defects create the 13 fA tail. Flip: put thin epitaxial Si on Kyropoulos sapphire, so the node has no substrate junction and leaks only through the channel. Sapphire boules use molybdenum crucibles, not high-purity quartz.
why: Refresh (fact 3): removes the junction/GIDL tail for ~10x retention, on a substrate independent of Spruce Pine.

title: Prefab cleanroom pods add DRAM capacity in $500M steps
idea: Constraint: capital may arrive only in $500M increments. Factory-built cleanroom pods, each a complete array-only line for ~2k wafer starts/month, are shipped and plugged into shared utilities and a partner logic fab for periphery, going from order to output in ~12 months.
why: Capital intensity and time: replaces $15B, 3-5-year lumpy bets with demand-matched modules, lowering financing risk and speeding a U.S. ramp.

title: Thermophoretic wafer shielding allows ISO-7 cleanrooms for DRAM fabs
idea: Effect: thermophoresis. Every exposed wafer is held 10-20 K warmer than the gas around it inside sealed carriers and tool mini-environments; the thermophoretic force pushes sub-100 nm particles away from the warm surface, cutting deposition velocity by more than 100x, so the ballroom can be ISO 7 instead of ISO 3-4.
why: Capital: cleanroom and facilities are ~20-30% of a $15B fab and a large energy load; a cheaper shell could save billions and about a year of U.S. fab construction.

title: Sell the ramp: defect-tolerant early-yield wafers
idea: Reverse 'ship only mature yield': during a new fab's ramp, sell lower-bin dies with published defect maps to AI training customers whose software already tolerates row retirement, so the ramp earns revenue instead of scrap.
why: Brings forward ~6-12 months of revenue on a $15B fab, which cuts net capital at risk and payback time for new U.S. capacity.

title: Dual-damascene fusion of storage-node contact and landing pad
idea: Combine BEOL dual-damascene with the DRAM buried-contact module: the storage-node contact hole and the landing-pad trench are etched into one stacked dielectric in a single trench-first/via-last sequence, then filled with one Ru or Mo deposition and planarized with one CMP.
why: Removes one critical EUV/SAQP patterning layer, one metal fill and one CMP from the 5-7 EUV-layer flow (fact 4), ~3-5% wafer cost; the Ru/Mo fill also cuts tungsten (China ~80%) exposure.

title: Eliminate per-product mask sets: one array die personalized late
idea: Design a single core array with interchangeable top-metal and fuse options so the same front-end wafers become DDR5 x4/x8, LPDDR5X or HBM core dies by choosing last-via masks late in the line. Each product still meets its unchanged JEDEC interface.
why: Capital: one front-end mask set instead of three (~$15-30M each with EUV), and output can swing between markets mid-flow, lifting fab utilization.

title: Solid-state 193 nm light sources remove neon and fluorine
idea: First principle: excimer gas is only a gain medium; 193 nm light can also come from frequency conversion of a ~1 um fiber laser through nonlinear crystals (harmonics plus sum-frequency mixing in CLBO/KBBF). Build a kW-class fiber-laser-pumped solid-state 193 nm source for immersion scanners with no neon/fluorine consumables, no gas-refill downtime and higher wall-plug efficiency.
why: Scarce resource (neon) and tool availability: higher DUV uptime makes DUV-heavy, EUV-free DRAM flows cheaper.

title: Jugaad engineer: indium-free zinc-tin oxide channels from abundant metals
idea: A jugaad engineer builds from what is plentiful. With indium supply concentrated in China, swap IGZO for indium- and gallium-free amorphous zinc-tin oxide (or Zn-Sn-Si-O) sputtered at room temperature from cheap targets, annealed at 300-350 C, and capped with a Si-rich back-channel layer that suppresses the off-current tail.
why: Removes indium and gallium supply risk from every oxide-semiconductor memory tier and cuts target cost ~3x. Risks: lower mobility (~10 cm2/Vs) and bias-stress stability.

title: Laser-induced periodic ripples: light self-organizes the grating
idea: Reverse projection imaging into self-organization: scan femtosecond laser pulses over a thin film to create laser-induced periodic surface structures with periods of lambda/5 to lambda/10, then transfer them as the array line grating.
why: Sub-50 nm gratings from a cheap fiber laser with no reticle and no EUV; laser tools cost ~1% of a scanner.

title: Metallurgist's layer exchange: aluminum-induced crystalline germanium periphery at 350 C
idea: Old metallurgists knew metals dissolve and reprecipitate semiconductors. Stack amorphous Ge over thin Al with a native-oxide barrier; at 300-350 C the Ge diffuses through the Al and recrystallizes beneath it as large-grain (>10 um), (111)-oriented film, giving high-mobility sense-amp and decoder transistors in tiers above the array.
why: Moves the periphery (49% of die, fact 7) above the array within 400 C, shrinking die area ~30-40% with no second front-end wafer. High risk: Al residue, grain-boundary leakage, threshold variation.

title: Femtosecond self-organized surface ripples pattern bitline gratings without resist
idea: Extreme user: a fab with no resist chemistry at all. Scan a femtosecond laser over a thin carbon or silicon hardmask so laser-induced periodic surface structures form self-organized ripples at ~lambda/4 pitch, locked into order by a seed grating, then transfer with Cl2/O2.
why: Litho: chemical-free, maskless 1D grating patterning at high throughput; could remove both resist and masks from array line layers.

title: Holographic-grating interference lithography for the periodic cell lattice
idea: Adapt diffraction-grating and security-hologram production: print the strictly periodic array layers with three-beam 193 nm interference or displacement Talbot lithography (one periodic phase mask scanned in z), which writes hexagonal hole lattices across a full field with near-unlimited depth of focus and no projection lens; a cheap KrF trim exposure clears the array edges.
why: EUV dependence and scanner capex (fact 4): interference tools cost ~$5-15M versus $200M+ for EUV, need no product reticle, and with one spacer pitch split reach array pitch; claim ~3 EUV layers removed.

title: Revive IBM-heritage deep-trench eDRAM as hot-rated standalone memory
idea: Under 125 C for 10 years: license the existing SOI deep-trench eDRAM process (~25-40 fF cells) held by a U.S. foundry and productize it as standalone 125 C DRAM in its New York fabs, with no new tool or process development.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: large-Cs trenches meet hot retention immediately, near-zero new capex, months not years to first product.

title: Movable-type reticles: tile-stepped array masks shared across products
idea: Like Gutenberg composing pages from reusable type, write a small defect-free array-tile reticle (one mat) and step it repeatedly inside a bladed field, then expose periphery from a type case of standard sense-amp, decoder and I/O tiles; new densities are composed from existing tiles instead of new full reticles.
why: Mask cost/cycle time: small tiles are cheaper and higher-yield to write; derivative mask-set cost falls ~50-70% and tape-out-to-wafer shrinks by weeks.

title: Catalytic metal-assisted etching drills 3D DRAM holes, no plasma
idea: First principle: plasma etch rate collapses with depth because ions and neutrals must reach the hole bottom (Knudsen transport), whereas metal-assisted chemical etching dissolves Si only at the catalyst/Si interface, so its rate does not depend on depth. Imprint Au or Pt nanodots on an epitaxial Si/SiGe superlattice and let them sink through 100+ tiers in HF/H2O2 to form the vertical bitline and channel holes of a 3D DRAM.
why: 3D DRAM blocker (fact 2) and etch capex: a wet bench replaces cryo-etch tools (~$5-8M each) and reaches tier counts where plasma etch stalls.

title: Offset-cancelled sense amps shrink the capacitor to AR 20:1
idea: First principle: a cell must store only enough charge to beat the sense amp's offset, dV = (Vdd/2)*Cs/(Cs+Cbl) > ~3 sigma_offset. Put auto-zeroed, offset-cancelling sense amps under the array (bonded CMOS) and cut bitline length 4x so Cbl falls; then a ~1.5 fF cell built at AR ~20:1 with standard etch replaces the AR 70:1 pillar.
why: Capacitor wall and etch capex (facts 1, 4): removes the hardest high-AR etch and mold module; ~10-15% fewer process steps and higher yield.

title: Repeated smart-cut transfers stack single-crystal transistor tiers with donor reuse
idea: Effect: hydrogen-platelet exfoliation. Implanted H forms a cleave plane, so 100-200 nm single-crystal Si layers are bonded and split one at a time onto a cold DRAM wafer; each tier's lateral access transistors are patterned before the next bond. Donor wafers are re-polished and reused 10+ times.
why: Facts 2 and 3: single-crystal channels have a smaller leakage tail than deposited poly or oxide, the SiGe epi superlattice goes away, and donor reuse saves silicon and HP-quartz-crucible capacity.

title: Layer-by-layer perovskite nanosheets give k-200 dielectric for shallow capacitors
idea: Effect: giant 2D dielectric polarizability plus electrostatic self-assembly. Alternate dips in polycation and exfoliated Ca2Nb3O10 or Sr2Nb3O10 nanosheets (k ~200 at ~10 nm) coat low-AR holes at room temperature. With k about 5x that of ZrO2 stacks, 5 fF fits in a ~12-15:1 hole.
why: Fact 1 asks for k ~70; this beats it, so AR drops from 60-75 to ~15 and the HAR etch, support mesh and collapse-control steps go away. Room-temperature wet processing on cheap tools.

title: Par-baked bread: split DRAM front-end and finishing across fabs
idea: Borrowed from par-baked bread shipped from central bakeries to stores: leading fabs ship wafers with transistors, wordlines and bitlines done; regional U.S. finishing fabs add capacitors, top metals, test and packaging using only 193 nm dry litho, ALD and etch, splitting a ~90-day flow into two ~45-day hops.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: a finishing fab needs ~1/5 the capex and no EUV, captures ~40% of the process value and adds surge capacity close to customers.

title: Glass-coated microwire twistors woven into memory fabric on looms
idea: Revive Bell Labs' 1957 twistor (helically magnetized tape wound on a wire) using Taylor-Ulitovsky glass-coated CoFeSiB microwires, already drawn by the kilometre at 5-20 um diameter, given helical anisotropy by torsion annealing; an industrial loom weaves them with copper word straps into a fabric whose crossings are bits, read by giant magneto-impedance. No wafer, litho or vacuum tool touches the array.
why: Capital intensity: a microwire tower plus loom costs ~$1-5M and can run anywhere in the U.S.; density is low (~1-10 Mb/cm2 per layer), so the step change is capital per bit for a refresh-free capacity tier, not leading-edge cost per bit.

title: Eliminate whole-stack scrap: a hot-spare core die inside each HBM stack
idea: Bond 13 core dies for a 12-high HBM3E stack; the base die tests each layer after bonding and steers a failed die's channels to the spare through a crossbar, so the GPU sees a standard 12-high device.
why: Fact 6: stack losses of 20-30% (one bad die kills the stack) fall to a few percent, worth far more than the ~8% extra die cost.

title: Washing machine: metal-assisted wet etching drills AR>100 capacitor holes
idea: Random stimulus 'washing machine' (a wet bath does the work) -> a patterned noble-metal mesh on silicon catalyzes local oxidation and dissolution in HF/H2O2, so the mesh sinks straight down and leaves a hole array with AR >100. Room-temperature wet tanks replace the plasma high-AR etch.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1) and capital: high-AR dielectric etch tools are among the costliest in the fab. MacEtch reaches very high aspect ratios with no plasma, so Cs could grow ~1.5x and etch capex fall >5x.

title: Water-droplet capillary self-alignment stacks DRAM dies without thermocompression bonders
idea: Effect: surface-tension energy minimization. Pattern hydrophilic pads inside hydrophobic surrounds on the dies; a coarse, ~$150k used pick-and-place drops each die onto a water film, and capillary force pulls it to <1 um alignment within ~100 ms before direct bonding. A 24-month, $1M program demonstrates 4-high wide-I/O stacks.
why: Fact 6: HBM stacking uses $3-5M TCB or hybrid bonders with slow per-die alignment; parallel capillary alignment could cut stacking capex per unit ~5-10x.

title: Interleaved product codes let array layers run in ISO-5 bays
idea: Combine particle-defect statistics with 2D-interleaved product codes in which each codeword spans cells at least 1 um apart in both axes, and with segmented wordlines and bitlines, so a killer particle costs one symbol per codeword. Less critical array back-end layers then run in ISO-5 bays rather than ISO-3 minienvironments.
why: Cleanroom build is ~15-20% of fab capex and HVAC is a major energy draw; a relaxed class cuts that slice ~30% (capital intensity, energy).

title: Minienvironment-only DRAM fab with defect-tolerant wafer-scale sparing
idea: Box: standard cell x standard access x self-testing sense with built-in repair x wafer-scale integration x Si x sealed-FOUP and tool-minienvironment fab in an ISO-6 shell. Arrays carry 10-15% spare subarrays and on-die BIST remaps defective rows at power-up, so the higher particle density of a cheap building is absorbed by architecture rather than by an ISO-1 ballroom.
why: Capital intensity: the cleanroom building is ~20-30% of fab capex; an ISO-6 shell could halve it and cut 1-2 years of construction, at a cost of ~10% array area for spares.

title: Thermoplastic, solvent-release packages make DRAM dies recoverable
idea: First principle: epoxy molding compound is a thermoset that cannot be undone, so it traps the die forever. Package DRAM in a high-Tg thermoplastic (e.g., liquid-crystal polymer) with a solvent-releasable underfill, so a low-temperature solvent bath frees bare, intact dies for retest and redeployment.
why: Recyclability: die-level reuse plus gold/copper recovery; feeds reverse-fab supply.

title: Eliminate the silicon wafer: DRAM on Gen-8.5 display glass panels
idea: Build 12-16 tiers of oxide-TFT gain cells at F~0.5 um on 2.2 x 2.5 m glass in under-used LCD/OLED fabs, which already own panel-scale litho, sputter and PECVD. One panel has ~60x the area of a 300 mm wafer, so even at coarse F it holds ~3-7 TB of capacity-tier memory behind a CXL-style controller.
why: Capital and crucible chokepoint: display-fab capex per m2 is ~50-100x lower than a DRAM fab, with no Czochralski silicon, quartz crucible or EUV; targets ~$1-3/GB for a slower (~100 ns) tier that frees real DRAM for hot data.

title: Eliminate per-die probe touchdowns: scribe-line test bus, one contact per wafer
idea: Wire every die to a shared power and serial test bus routed through the scribe lines to a few large edge pads; one touchdown powers all dies, each runs BIST and reports over the bus, and a fuse isolates shorted dies. Dicing cuts the bus away, leaving standard DDR5/HBM dies.
why: Replaces fine-pitch probe cards and multi-touchdown sort with one cheap contact; ~10x sort throughput and no probe marks on hybrid-bond pads.

title: Light-powered, contactless wafer-level DRAM test
idea: First principle: a retention test needs only power, a clock and a readout, and all three can be optical. Put a photodiode power island and a micro-LED or optical modulator on each die, flood-light the whole wafer so every die runs BIST march and retention tests in parallel, and read pass/fail maps with a camera, replacing probe cards and most testers.
why: Test capital and throughput: DRAM testers and probe cards are billions of dollars of capex; full-wafer parallel test in minutes.

title: Eliminate wide scribes: in-die test structures, plasma dicing, 10 um streets
idea: Move process-control monitors and alignment marks into dummy areas inside the die, shrink scribe streets from ~60-80 um to ~10 um, and singulate by plasma dicing; dies are unchanged JEDEC DDR5/HBM parts.
why: Adds ~3-6% gross dies per wafer and removes saw-kerf chipping on thin HBM dies, a free capacity gain.

title: Printmaker's mask-free interference lithography for crossed array gratings
idea: An etching artist makes plates by interfering beams, not by drawing. Expose array line and hole layers with 193 nm immersion two-beam interference lithography, a mask-free, lens-free tool that writes a ~70 nm-pitch grating across the whole wafer in one flash; two rotated exposures form a hole lattice, and one spacer doubling reaches DRAM pitch, aligned through the moire between the grating and a reference mark.
why: No reticles and no projection optics: a ~$5-10M laser-and-mirror tool replaces immersion or EUV passes on periodic layers, with throughput set by laser power rather than stage scanning. Claim ~50% less litho capex on array layers.

title: Double-sided wafers: native two-high stacks on both faces
idea: Worse: use only one face of every expensive crystal wafer. Flip: run FEOL on both faces in edge-gripped double-sided tools. Furnace anneals and blanket depositions treat both faces in one pass, while litho alternates sides. TSVs then link the faces into a native two-high die stack without any bonding step.
why: Bits per wafer start ~1.8x with shared thermal/deposition steps; crucible-limited substrate use per bit roughly halves; HBM gets one bond layer free.

title: Brighton-rock drawn preform sliced into ready-made capacitor wafers
idea: Like seaside rock candy whose lettering is built large and drawn thin, stack a 10 cm glass preform holding thousands of coaxial metal/glass/metal rods, draw and re-stack-draw it (fiber-optic faceplate practice) ~10^5x down to ~40 nm pitch, then saw and polish 10 um slices carrying billions of coaxial capacitors to bond onto transistor wafers.
why: Facts 1 and 4: zero lithography and zero HAR etch for the capacitor; a 10 um-tall coax gives ~6 fF even with glass k~8 because its effective aspect ratio is ~250:1; one preform yields thousands of slices.

title: Steel minimill playbook: EUV-free DRAM on used DUV plus stacking
idea: Borrowed from Nucor's electric-arc minimills, which beat integrated mills starting with low-end rebar: build a $2-3B U.S. DRAM minimill on used ArF-immersion scanners at ~18-20 nm half-pitch with SAQP and no EUV, close the density gap by hybrid-bonding several array wafers over one periphery wafer, and sell first into industrial and auto DDR4/LPDDR4 that incumbents are exiting.
why: Capital and U.S. manufacturability: ~5x less capex per wafer start than an EUV fab, with density recovered by stacking; enter low, move up.

title: Eliminate periphery and product layout from array wafers: universal lattice wafers
idea: Fabricate wafers that hold nothing but an endless, product-agnostic cell lattice (no decoders, sense amps or I/O), then hybrid-bond them wafer-to-wafer onto separately made logic wafers that define product, banking and die boundaries; die size is chosen at dicing.
why: Facts 4 and 7: the array fab needs ~40% fewer masks and no product-specific reticles, runs one recipe at full utilization, and periphery moves to a cheaper logic process; ~20-30% cost-per-bit gain.

title: Zero-EUV array: one grating mask plus spacer cascade
idea: Constraint: no EUV anywhere in the array. Print a single ~80 nm-pitch ArF-immersion grating per direction and derive active, buried wordline, bitline and storage-node contacts by self-aligned spacer quadrupling with tone inversion at the crossings, leaving only two relaxed-pitch cut masks at the array edge.
why: Fact 4: removes the 5-7 EUV exposures and ~60% of array masks; est. -25-35% wafer cost and no dependence on the single EUV supplier.

title: Contactless charge-shift KV-cache memory printed with gratings only
idea: Extreme user: AI KV-cache, written sequentially and read in streams. Store it in a CCD-like charge-transfer register (parallel gate lines over a buried channel clocked to shift packets to an edge sense amp) with no per-cell contacts, capacitors or vias, so every dense layer is a 1D grating printable by immersion SAQP or nanoimprint.
why: Litho/capital: zero EUV layers, ~50% fewer masks, ~2F^2 per bit, and no capacitor module; ideal for the sequential KV share of AI memory demand.

title: Chemistry is the mask: area-selective deposition of landing pads
idea: Reverse 'litho decides where material goes': passivate oxide with self-assembled monolayer inhibitors so ALD metal only nucleates on exposed contact plugs, growing storage-node landing pads in place with no lithography.
why: Removes the landing-pad layer, one of the critical EUV layers in leading DRAM, and its overlay budget.

title: Substitute diced packaged memory with wafer-on-wafer bonding and redundancy routing
idea: Bond a whole DRAM wafer to a whole accelerator wafer without dicing, and route around defective DRAM tiles through a configurable redundancy fabric on the logic side, so no known-good-die test or per-die packaging is needed.
why: Constraint: 1-2 um bond pitch gives ~0.1 pJ/bit at TB/s per mm2 (>=30x below HBM); capital: eliminates dicing, KGD test, TSVs, interposers and substrates (fact 6).

title: Garage-fab DMD maskless printers expose DRAM's non-critical layers
idea: Extreme user: hobbyist and university garage fabs that cannot afford masks. Use digital-micromirror maskless exposure (like PCB direct imaging, upgraded to ~150 nm with 4x reduction optics) for the ~40% of DRAM layers above 200 nm (implants, pads, thick metals, periphery wells).
why: Masks: cuts ~$3-6M of mask-set cost per product, enables same-day design spins and SKU variants without mask lead times.

title: Nanoimprint arrays with non-fluorinated hydrocarbon release layers
idea: Extreme user: medical-sensor makers who already require PFAS-free supply chains. Print DRAM array layers by jet-and-flash nanoimprint whose quartz templates use octadecyl-silane or DLC anti-stick coatings instead of fluorosilanes, with a shrink-releasing resin.
why: Litho capital: nanoimprint tools cost ~1/10 of EUV scanners for periodic arrays; removing fluorinated release agents clears the PFAS barrier to adoption.

title: Self-ordered anodic alumina as a litho-free capacitor template
idea: Revive Keller's 1950s porous-alumina work and Masuda's 1995 two-step anodization: aluminium e-beam evaporated over the bitline layer (no Ar sputtering) is anodized in oxalic or sulfuric acid into hexagonally ordered pores at 40-60 nm pitch and >100:1 AR, registered to landing pads by a shallow imprinted pit pattern. Pores are lined by N2-purged ALD TiN/ZrO2/TiN to form capacitors.
why: Facts 1 and 4: removes the capacitor-hole SAQP/EUV patterning and the high-AR plasma etch (~2 critical layers, ~10 steps) with a room-temperature wet tool and no rare gas; AR >100 gives Cs >=8 fF. Risks are pore defects and pad registration.

title: Notch-guided crack propagation cuts sub-10 nm isolation gaps without cut masks
idea: Effect: controlled brittle fracture. Deposit a brittle, tensile SiNx film and use cheap i-line litho to place micro-notches; cracks start at the notches and run straight along designed stress channels, leaving 5-10 nm gaps that become word-line or active-area cuts. $1M on 150 mm wafers over 24 months measures straightness and placement accuracy.
why: Fact 4: DRAM cut and trim layers need EUV or multiple patterning; crack-defined cuts give sub-10 nm gaps from i-line tools, saving an EUV layer if placement holds.

title: Zn: vapor-grown zinc MOF films as dry-developed resist
idea: Convert an ALD ZnO film into a ZIF-8 metal-organic framework by exposure to 2-methylimidazole vapor; e-beam/EUV exposure alters the framework so a reactive gas removes exposed or unexposed areas, giving a solvent-free, water-free, metal-rich resist.
why: Water: removes the wet track (spin, develop, rinse) from each litho layer, >10x water and solvent reduction for that module, with higher etch resistance than organic resists.

title: Metal-assisted chemical etching drills capacitor holes at wet-bench cost
idea: TRIZ #28 Mechanics substitution replaces the ion field with a catalytic chemical one: pattern a noble-metal catalyst dot lattice, immerse in HF/H2O2, and each dot sinks vertically into silicon carving 100:1 holes for buried capacitors or vertical-channel transistors, 50 wafers per batch.
why: Wet bench ~$1-3M vs ~$5-10M+ per HAR etch chamber plus chillers; batch processing raises deep-etch throughput ~10x (fact 4, capital).

title: Shipworm catalytic drilling replaces plasma etch for 200-tier holes
idea: Shipworms bore by chemistry rather than force; place Au or Pt catalyst discs, defined by the single hole lithography, on top of a 200-tier Si/SiGe stack and run metal-assisted chemical etching in HF/H2O2 so each disc sinks straight down, drilling ~30 nm holes at >500:1 aspect in a wet bench.
why: High-AR hole etch is the most capital-intensive 3D step and caps tier count; a MACE bench costs ~1/20 of a cryogenic etcher and goes deeper, so 150-200 tiers (~10x+ bits/mm2) arrive at about flat wafer cost (fact 2).

title: Catalyst nanodots burrow into silicon to drill capacitor holes
idea: Po: the hole digs itself. Place Pt or Ag nanodots by imprint or self-assembly and run metal-assisted chemical etching in HF/H2O2: each dot sinks straight down, giving AR >100:1 holes in a wet bench; strip catalyst and line with high-k for trench-type storage capacitors.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1) and etch capex: wet bench ~1/20 the cost of a high-AR plasma etcher; AR >100 without bowing for Cs >8 fF.

title: Substitute investor capital with customer-prepaid ten-year bit-supply notes
idea: Hyperscalers prepay for guaranteed exabits per year through a tradable 'bit-supply note' tied to one specific fab line, priced cost-plus with an index; the fab's capital comes from those who most fear the shortage.
why: Capital intensity: moves $15B+ of risk off the memory maker's balance sheet, shortens time-to-decision, and damps the boom-bust underinvestment behind the 4x price spike.

title: Four-level cells read by time-to-threshold sensing
idea: Inverts 'a DRAM cell stores one binary bit'. Store four charge levels per large 180 nm-rule cell (~30 fF) and read by timing how long the bitline takes to cross a reference, with a ramp and counter shared per mat and reference cells rewritten each refresh to cancel leakage drift.
why: Doubles bits per mask step at fixed litho; big old-node capacitors give MLC the margin modern 5 fF cells lack (facts 1, 4).

title: Quarter-dose EUV exposures quadruple scanner throughput, stochastics absorbed
idea: Combine EUV exposure with error-tolerant cells: the contact and capacitor-hole layers are exposed at ~15 mJ/cm2 instead of ~60, and the resulting photon-shot-noise missing or merged features (~0.1-1% of cells) are accepted as cell errors handled by the code layer.
why: EUV throughput is dose-limited, so ~3-4x more wafers per scanner-hour cuts EUV cost per layer ~60% and the number of scarce single-supplier scanners needed (fact 4).

title: Substitute helium backside cooling with electrolyzer hydrogen and closed-loop capture
idea: Run electrostatic-chuck backside cooling in etch, CVD and implant tools with 5-20 Torr hydrogen (higher thermal conductivity than helium) from an on-site electrolyzer, and fit remaining helium uses (leak check, purge, litho) with cryogenic capture-and-reuse loops. Chuck seals get diffusion barriers so exhaust stays well under the H2 lower explosive limit.
why: Helium chokepoint (Qatar ~30%, offline since March 2026): cuts fab helium draw >80%, decoupling DRAM output from helium shocks.

title: Debondable hybrid-bond layer lets you swap the bad HBM tier
idea: First principle: stack yield falls as y^n because one bad die kills the stack; if the bond is reversible, a failure costs one die instead. Bond Cu pads through a thin indium or Sn-Bi interlayer, with a dielectric that softens near 200 C, so a stack with one failed die is locally reheated, split and rebonded with a known-good die.
why: HBM yield tax (fact 6, 20-30% lost): recovers most failed stacks; ~20% lower capital per good bit.

title: Talbot self-imaging lithography for perfectly periodic arrays
idea: Exploit that the DRAM array is a perfect lattice: minify the optics to zero by using lensless Talbot/interference self-imaging of a periodic grating, magnifying the coherent print area to the full wafer for all array layers.
why: Litho capital: lens-free optics cost <5% of a scanner; 193 nm interference can print ~40 nm pitch lattices with infinite depth of focus, and periphery stays on cheap DUV.

title: Talbot self-imaging with solid-state deep-UV lasers prints periodic arrays
idea: Revive Talbot's 1836 self-imaging effect: a periodic mask under coherent light reproduces itself at fixed distances, and averaging over one Talbot period (displacement Talbot) prints half-pitch features with nearly unlimited depth of focus. Use a 193-213 nm all-solid-state frequency-multiplied laser, with no ArF excimer and no neon buffer gas, for DRAM capacitor and active-area grids.
why: Fact 4 under the constraint: a lens-free proximity tool at ~$5-10M versus ~$60M immersion scanners for periodic layers, with free pitch halving. Risks are solid-state DUV power and defects in regular arrays.

title: Kaleidoscope: tabletop EUV Talbot self-imaging for periodic array layers
idea: Random stimulus 'kaleidoscope' (repeating images from simple optics) -> achromatic Talbot lithography: a compact 13.5 nm source shines through a simple transmission grating mask, and the self-imaging effect reproduces the periodic line/hole pattern at a set gap with no projection optics. It is used only for the fully periodic array layers; DUV handles cuts and periphery.
why: EUV single-supplier chokepoint and capital (fact 4): a mirror-less exposure tool could cost ~1/10 of a scanner and needs no reflective-mask infrastructure. It suits DRAM's array layers, which are almost perfectly periodic.

title: Talbot self-imaging prints the cell lattice with U.S. lasers
idea: Displacement Talbot lithography: a 1:1 periodic phase mask from a U.S. mask shop and a U.S.-built 213/266 nm solid-state laser self-image the lattice across the whole wafer with near-unlimited depth of focus; no projection optics, so no imported scanner.
why: Removes EUV/ArF scanner dependence (single-supplier chokepoint) for array layers (Fact 4) with a ~$3-8M domestic tool.

title: Displacement-Talbot self-imaging prints periodic cell arrays without projection optics
idea: Effect: Talbot self-imaging. A periodic phase mask lit at 193 nm re-images itself at Talbot planes; sweeping the mask-wafer gap (displacement Talbot) averages out depth sensitivity and prints 36-40 nm-pitch honeycomb landing-pad and storage-node arrays across a full field in one flash. Only the aperiodic periphery goes to a scanner, and dummy rows at the array edge absorb the Talbot edge defects.
why: Litho capital (fact 4): the core array is ~51% of the die and perfectly periodic, so 1-2 of the 5-7 EUV layers move to a ~$3-5M mask-aligner-class tool; claimed 30-50% lower litho cost for those layers.

title: Two-level nanoimprint stamp, like CD replication, for node and pad
idea: Borrowed from CD/DVD plants, which mold multi-depth pit structures in one shot: make a two-level quartz imprint template carrying both landing-pad and storage-node levels, so one jet-and-flash imprint replaces two critical exposures and their overlay step, the way dual damascene merged via and trench.
why: Fact 4: removes 1-2 EUV/193i-multipatterning layers per die from the array; NIL tool ~1/3 the price of EUV and self-aligned levels eliminate one overlay error budget.

title: Spatial ALD-ALE supercycles sculpt capacitor holes in one tool
idea: Combine spatial (rotary-platen) atomic layer deposition with atomic layer etching on one platen. Alternating sectors deposit a protective liner at the hole top and quasi-isotropically etch the bowed and tapered zones, reshaping each high-aspect-ratio hole into a straight cylinder in one pass.
why: Replaces separate etch-deposit-etch profile-correction loops across 3-4 tools. Straight walls give ~20% more Cs at the same AR (fact 1) and ~15% fewer chamber-hours.

title: National nanofab DRAM shuttle with an open cell PDK
idea: Box: business/policy axis set to distributed prototyping. Fund an NNCI-style shuttle where a standardized 150 mm open DRAM cell flow (contact litho, EBL, ALD, sputter only) runs quarterly in ten university nanofabs with shared test chips, open PDK and characterization, so startups test new cells for ~$50k in months instead of $5-10M.
why: U.S. manufacturability and time-to-innovation: widens the funnel of new cell concepts using fabs that already exist; risk is translation from 150 mm university flows to 300 mm production.

title: FOUPs that pre-clean wafers while traveling between tools
idea: Combine overhead automated transport with a vapor-phase process chamber: smart FOUPs with onboard N2 purge, HF-vapor native-oxide removal and UV dehydration run queue-time-critical pre-clean steps in transit. Time-linked sequences then no longer need dedicated tool clusters.
why: Queue-time constraints idle ~5-10% of DRAM tool capacity and force tool duplication; in-transit processing reclaims it (capital intensity, throughput).

title: Gas-storage MOF chemistry: zinc-imidazolate vapor-deposited photoresist
idea: Borrow zeolitic imidazolate frameworks (ZIF-8) from gas separation: grow the resist by vapor-phase conversion of an ALD ZnO film into ZIF-8 (Zn, C, H, N), which decomposes under EUV, DUV or e-beam and develops in vapor, replacing Sn-, Hf- or Zr-based metal-oxide EUV resists and spin tracks.
why: EUV throughput (fact 4): Zn absorbs EUV far better than organic resists, so lower dose and more wafers per scanner-hour; solvent-free conformal coating; no Hf.

title: Eliminate liquid drying and support lattices: vapor-HF release plus supercritical CO2
idea: Remove the capacitor mold oxide with vapor-phase HF and rinse/dry in supercritical CO2, so tall pillars never see a liquid-vapor meniscus and need none of the nitride support lattices added today to stop leaning and stiction.
why: Fact 1: removes 2-3 support-layer deposition/litho/etch loops and lets AR rise from ~70 to ~115:1 without collapse (~50% more Cs), while cutting water use.

title: P: vapor phosphonate monolayer doping replaces implant-and-strip loops
idea: Form a phosphorus-bearing self-assembled monolayer from the vapor phase on Si exposed through a reusable hardmask (not resist), cap it and spike-anneal to drive a shallow conformal dopant profile, even inside 3D tunnels that implant beams cannot reach.
why: Water: each implant layer (10+ in DRAM) normally needs resist coat, strip and clean; vapor doping removes that water (>10x for the doping module) and enables doping of lateral 3D cells.

title: Defense-trusted DRAM uses chloride-precursor molybdenum wordlines, no WF6
idea: Extreme user: defense buyers who must avoid Chinese tungsten and fluorinated gases. Replace WF6-CVD tungsten buried wordlines and contacts with molybdenum from MoO2Cl2/H2, barrier-less, and run a chlorine-only metal stack.
why: Scarce resource: removes the ~80% China tungsten exposure and WF6; barrier-less Mo also cuts wordline resistance ~30% for finer pitch.

title: High-pressure deuterium anneal heals leakage tails in downgraded DRAM wafers
idea: Effect: isotope-hardened dangling-bond passivation. Buy downgraded or scrap DRAM wafers from brokers before dicing and anneal them at ~400 C in a used 10-20 atm D2 furnace (~$400k): deuterium passivates the interface and GIDL trap centers behind the leakage tail, and Si-D bonds are ~10x more stable than Si-H. Re-test and resell recovered dies; the rest of the $1M funds test and 24 months of qualification.
why: Fact 3: trims the <=13 fA tail that sets refresh failures; recovered dies add supply with no new fab.

title: Atmospheric mist-CVD oxide channels for error-tolerant gain cells
idea: Combine atmospheric ultrasonic mist-CVD, as used for Ga2O3 and solar TCOs, with 2T gain cells: the In-Ga-Zn-O-like channel is deposited without vacuum sputtering or ALD, and ~1% of cells with off-current outliers are absorbed by the code layer.
why: Vacuum tools cost $3-8M each, while mist-CVD tools are ~10x cheaper with higher throughput, cutting BEOL memory-tier capex (capital intensity, U.S. manufacturability).

title: Plumber's capillary self-alignment: water-droplet HBM die stacking
idea: A plumber knows water finds its level. Drop HBM dies coarsely (+/-20 um) onto hydrophilic bond sites carrying a water microdroplet; surface tension pulls each die into <1 um alignment within milliseconds, then evaporation and one collective hybrid-bond anneal fix every die at once.
why: Replaces slow precision thermocompression/pick-and-place bonders (~1-2k UPH, ~$3M each) with fast coarse placement (>10k UPH) and a batch anneal, attacking the HBM stacking tax (fact 6). Risks: particles, water residue and bond voids.

title: Liquid-metal microbumps make memory stacks hot-swappable
idea: First principle: solder joints are permanent because they solidify, while gallium-indium-tin eutectic stays liquid above ~11 C and wets only treated pads. Connect DRAM dies to a base die through Galinstan-filled micro-wells sealed by a polymer gasket and held by a mechanical clamp, so dies can be pulled, tested and replaced at room temperature.
why: Repairability and yield: known-good stacks after assembly and die reuse at end of life, with no reflow damage.

title: Zoned newspaper editions: consortium base wafers, one personalization mask
idea: Like papers that print a common edition and swap one plate per zone, a consortium fab runs one standardized DRAM base wafer (array, sense amps, generic I/O) at maximum volume, and each buyer personalizes it with exactly one metal/via mask (density cut, interface, I/O width) on its own BEOL line.
why: Capital: hyperscale volume on one base flow lowers cost per bit, and new entrants need only a ~$0.5-1B BEOL line instead of a $15B fab.

title: Electroless bottom-up fill for wordlines and contacts, no sputtering
idea: Revive Brenner and Riddell's 1946 electroless plating: grow buried wordlines and bitline contacts bottom-up from a Pd-colloid-seeded floor with autocatalytic Co-B or Ni-B and a self-assembled monolayer diffusion barrier, so neither an Ar-sputtered TiN liner nor tungsten CVD is needed. The bath fills high-AR trenches without voids.
why: The constraint plus scarcity: removes argon PVD and the tungsten (China ~80%) in buried wordlines and contacts, using ~$2M baths instead of ~$10M PVD/CVD clusters. Risks are resistivity and work-function control in the buried wordline.

title: Double-angle shadow evaporation sets 20 nm channels without fine lithography
idea: Box: oxide-node charge x lateral oxide TFT whose source-drain gap is set by evaporation angle x current sensing x 2D x glass or Si x Dolan resist bridge plus two tilted e-beam evaporations, borrowed from superconducting-qubit junction fab. The gap equals bridge height times the tangent difference of the two angles, so a ~200 nm optical feature yields a ~20 nm self-aligned channel.
why: Sidesteps litho-bound scaling (fact 4): the critical dimension comes from angle and film thickness, not resolution; any university evaporator with a tilt stage works; risk is wafer-scale angle uniformity.

title: Clonal-selection redundancy lets cheaper, sloppier lithography make DRAM
idea: The immune system over-produces clones and keeps those that fit; design arrays with 15-20% spare rows/columns in fine 64-cell remap units, deliberately relax CD/overlay specs so 2-3 EUV layers move to ArF quad patterning at higher defect density, and let on-die test select working segments and burn the map into an antifuse bank.
why: Trades ~15% area for removing EUV layers and the tight defect spec; est. 15-25% lower wafer cost and ~10% lower cost per bit (fact 4).

title: Beaker-grown anodic Nb/Ta/Hf oxide as the capacitor dielectric
idea: Box: barrier-type anodic oxide charge x EBL-patterned IGZO access x standard sensing x 2D test array x Si x room-temperature electrochemical anodization of a sputtered valve metal. The bottom electrode's surface is anodized at ~1.5-2 nm/V into a dense dielectric (Nb2O5 k~40, Ta2O5 k~25) whose thickness is set by a voltage and whose pinholes self-heal during growth.
why: Removes the ALD tool from the dielectric step and self-heals defects for yield; buildable with a potentiostat and wet bench; risk is anodic-oxide leakage below 5 nm and contacting the electrode during anodization.

title: Z-RAM revived on GAA nanosheets: free floating bodies, no SOI
idea: Innovative Silicon's Z-RAM died on costly SOI wafers and a floating-body signal that shrank with scaling. Gate-all-around nanosheet stacks, already standard in logic fabs, are naturally floating bodies: write holes into 3-4 stacked sheets per cell by gate-induced drain leakage and sense the summed current shift, giving capacitorless DRAM with ~2 extra masks in any GAA foundry.
why: Deletes the capacitor module (AR 60-75 mold etch, high-k ALD, ~5-7 litho/etch steps) and the SOI premium; multi-sheet summing restores the margin that killed Z-RAM; lets U.S. GAA logic fabs build DRAM-class macros. Claimed ~30-40% fewer array process steps.

title: Se: xerographic charge-image patterning with dry nanoparticle toner
idea: Coat the wafer with a thin amorphous-selenium photoconductor, corona-charge it, expose with patterned light so charge leaks where lit, then cascade charged hardmask nanoparticles that stick only to the charge image; fuse, etch and sublime away the Se.
why: Water and capital: dry, solvent-free patterning on copier-class tooling for coarse periphery/BEOL layers (100s of nm), ~100x cheaper litho for those layers. Resolution is the risk.

title: Quilter's patchwork: collective nanotwinned-copper die bonding at 200 C
idea: A quilter sews all the patches at once. Stack memory dies on (111)-oriented nanotwinned copper pads, which bond by fast surface diffusion at 150-200 C: tack-place a whole wafer of die stacks quickly, then bond them all in one batch press.
why: A lower bond temperature reduces warpage and allows thinner dies; batch bonding raises stacking throughput ~5-10x and cuts bonder count, attacking the HBM stacking cost (fact 6). Risks: pad planarity and voids at <5 um pitch.

title: Blood-clotting repair: current-triggered electroless plating heals weak lines
idea: Platelets clot only at an injury; before final passivation, flood the wafer with an electroless Co or Ru bath and drive test current along every wordline and bitline so constrictions and thin spots heat locally, accelerating thermally activated plating exactly there until resistance normalizes.
why: Repairs near-open and high-resistance defects, a top yield killer at ~12 nm half-pitch; est. +3-6% yield, which also permits more aggressive, cheaper patterning.

title: Honeycomb: anodic alumina pores self-register on landing pads as capacitor molds
idea: Random stimulus 'honeycomb' -> an aluminum film deposited over the landing-pad array is anodized at ~10-12 V, so pores nucleate at the pad-induced topographic dimples and grow straight down as a self-ordered hexagonal array with aspect ratio >100. The pores serve as the storage-capacitor mold, which needs no lithography and no high-AR plasma etch.
why: Attacks the capacitor charge wall (fact 1: AR 115 needed) and capital (fact 4). The mold litho and the most expensive etch step become a wet electrochemical bench costing <$1M, and AR rises from 70 to 120+ for ~1.7x more Cs.

title: Tardigrade dormant-wafer banks absorb DRAM demand and price swings
idea: Tardigrades suspend metabolism and revive on demand; run wafers through the capital-heavy front end (array and capacitor) during demand troughs, park them in dry-nitrogen 'cryptobiosis' stockers, and finish BEOL and test in 3-4 weeks when prices spike.
why: Keeps EUV front ends near 95% utilization across the cycle and halves response time to shortages (fact 4); effectively 10-20% more output per dollar of capex.

title: Anodic aluminum oxide pores serve as the capacitor mold
idea: Combine electrochemical anodization (self-ordered AAO reaches aspect ratios above 200 in wet baths) with the DRAM capacitor. Al is deposited over the landing pads and imprint-textured so pores nucleate over each pad, anodized at room temperature into 15-20 nm pores 2-3 um deep, and the electrodes and dielectric are then ALD-coated inside.
why: Replaces the most capital-intensive DRAM tool, high-aspect-ratio plasma etch of the 60-75:1 mold, with bath processing. AR ~115 becomes reachable (fact 1) for ~+50% Cs, and module capex falls ~5x.

title: Image-sensor wafer-bond lines put capacitors on the backside
idea: Po: the wafer has two front sides. Use existing backside-illuminated image-sensor lines (wafer bonding, thinning to a few microns, backside litho) to flip a 40-65 nm transistor array and build tall capacitors on the freed backside, contacting drains through the thinned silicon so bitlines and capacitors stop competing for one side.
why: Capacitor wall and cell area (facts 1,7): front carries bitlines and periphery, back carries capacitors; near-4F2 layouts in trailing fabs with existing CIS tools.

title: Tunnel-diode SRAM revived with SiGe interband diodes in contacts
idea: Revive the 1960s Esaki tunnel-diode store and TI's 1990s tunneling SRAM (one transistor plus two series negative-resistance diodes) using CVD-grown Si/SiGe resonant interband tunnel diodes stacked inside the cell contact plug, so the bistable latch sits under the bitline contact. The cell is static at near-1T area, so the capacitor module is deleted.
why: Facts 1 and 3: removes the 60-75:1 capacitor pillar (~15-20 steps including the hardest dry etch) and all refresh, at ~8-10F2 vs 6F2. Risk is valley current: it must reach ~fA per cell for standby power to beat refresh.

title: Snow globe: core-shell magnetic nanoparticles settle into wells as bits
idea: Random stimulus 'snow globe' (particles settle where they belong) -> chemically synthesized FePt-core/MgO-shell nanoparticles (each one a high-anisotropy bit with its own tunnel barrier) are fluidically self-assembled into DUV-defined wells over fixed-layer electrodes, then top-contacted and written with thermally assisted spin torque.
why: Non-volatile MRAM-class bits made by beaker chemistry instead of MTJ sputter and etch tools. It could cut the magnetic-module capex >10x, with 10-year retention at 5 nm from FePt anisotropy.

title: Blu-ray replication lines injection-mold nanostructured capacitor templates
idea: Worse: let idle optical-disc factories rot while capacitor etch bottlenecks fabs. Flip: injection-mold high-temperature PEI/PEEK substrates from a nickel stamper carrying ~100 nm pit arrays at ~3 s per part. ALD low-temperature electrodes and high-k into the pits, then laminate an oxide-TFT layer on top.
why: Capital: stamper replication costs ~cents per part versus EUV plus high-AR etch, on reused disc lines.

title: Memory-only 450 mm wafers with a stripped-down tool set
idea: The G450C 450 mm program died around 2016 because toolmakers would not fund ~$20B of development against uncertain orders from three logic giants. DRAM uses far fewer distinct tool types than logic, so a memory-only 450 mm consortium with government cost share qualifies only ~40 tool types and pre-commits volume.
why: Throughput and capital per bit: 2.25x area per wafer pass; past wafer-size transitions cut cost per die ~30%; fewer, larger tools per bit lower fab capex per Gb.

title: Ca: lattice-matched CaF2/Si epitaxial superlattice for strain-free 3D tiers
idea: Grow alternating single-crystal Si and CaF2 layers (~0.6% mismatch) in one pump-down; CaF2 serves as tier isolation and as a sacrificial layer that etches with high selectivity to Si, avoiding the strain accumulation that caps SiGe/Si stacks.
why: Fact 2: strain-free stacking allows 50+ tiers in a single deposition run without relaxation defects, past the ~26-tier break-even.

title: Embargo improvisation: helium-free wafer chucks and closed-loop helium recovery
idea: With Qatar's helium offline, a Soviet-style engineer redesigns the etch/deposition chuck: hydrogen-argon backside gas, a micro-channel liquid-cooled ceramic puck and a higher-clamp Johnsen-Rahbek chuck to close the gap, plus per-tool membrane capture that recycles >90% of the helium still used for stage cooling and leak checks.
why: Cuts fab helium use ~80-95%, removing a concentrated-supply chokepoint that can idle tools. Risks: H2 safety, and the lower thermal conductivity of argon demands tighter wafer-to-chuck gap control.

title: Eliminate CMP: subtractive metal patterning plus flowable self-planarizing dielectric
idea: Pattern bitlines and landing pads by direct etch of blanket Ru or Mo instead of damascene, then gap-fill with flowable SiOC that self-levels and is etched back to an optical endpoint, removing chemical-mechanical polish steps.
why: Removes ~10-20 CMP steps, slurry and much ultrapure-water use plus dishing-driven yield loss; ~5-8% fewer tools.

title: Marangoni flow planarizes 3D DRAM tiers without chemical-mechanical polishing
idea: Effect: thermocapillary (Marangoni) flow. Spin a flowable siloxane and scan a laser line that sets up a surface-tension gradient, so liquid flows from hot high spots into cooler trenches and levels the topography before UV cure. A ~$250k scanned-laser coater on 100 mm wafers tests planarity over 26-tier stair topography within 24 months.
why: Fact 2: 3D DRAM tier stacks need many CMP steps ($5M tools, slurry, defects); thermocapillary leveling could replace a share of them.

title: Customer-owned tool fleet leased to the memory fab
idea: Reverse capital ownership: hyperscalers buy and own the scanners, etchers and deposition tools as a securitized asset pool and lease them to a fab operator under take-or-pay output contracts.
why: Capital intensity: moves ~55% depreciation off the memory maker's books, cuts its cost of capital and lets new U.S. entrants start with near-zero tool capex.

title: Eliminate EUV in the array: maskless DUV interference lithography lattices
idea: The cell array is a perfectly periodic lattice, so expose the wordline, bitline and capacitor-hole layers with a three-beam 193 nm immersion interference tool (no reticle, no projection optics), then halve or quarter the pitch with ALD spacers. One coarse DUV trim mask removes the lattice at array edges, where conventional DUV patterns the periphery.
why: Litho and capital (fact 4): replaces 5-7 EUV exposures with a reticle-free tool costing ~$10-20M vs ~$200M per EUV scanner; estimated 15-25% wafer-cost cut and no single-supplier EUV dependence.

title: HP memristor's forming and selector killers fixed in a depreciated fab
idea: HP Labs' TiO2 memristor (The Machine) died on per-cell electroforming, variability and a separate selector, with no fab partner after the SK hynix deal lapsed. Use a self-rectifying Ta2O5/TaOx bilayer with a built-in series-resistor film so each deck is formed by one global flood pulse, and build 32 decks at 40 nm with dry 193 nm litho, 2 bits/cell, in a fully depreciated 300 mm fab.
why: Meets 100x: no depreciation load (55% of normal wafer cost), no EUV, 32 decks x 2 bits; est. ~$0.1/GB. Trades: ~1e9 endurance needing wear-leveling, ~100 ns reads and us writes.

title: Accountant's frozen node: stop shrinking, depreciate tools over fifteen years
idea: An accountant sees depreciation at ~55% of wafer cost while each shrink buys only 10-20%. Freeze lithography at today's node and win bits only by stacking (tiers, bonding) and design (refresh, periphery), running a paid-off copy-exact tool set for 15 years instead of 5 and financing fabs like toll roads.
why: Halving the depreciation share cuts wafer cost ~25-30%, more than a node shrink buys; copy-exact capacity with a fixed tool list builds faster (~2 years) and cheaper. Risk: rivals that keep shrinking; density must come from stacking.

title: Eliminate CVD electrodes: electroless ruthenium plating inside capacitor holes
idea: Seed the capacitor mold holes with a palladium-activated monolayer and electrolessly plate conformal Ru bottom and top electrodes from a wet bath, replacing CVD/ALD TiN.
why: Capital: plating cells cost a fraction of ALD/CVD chambers at higher throughput, and Ru's higher work function cuts dielectric leakage, allowing thinner high-k and more Cs.
